y6-1: Tai chi is a generally safe and practical option, and a fine example of an Eastern movement tradition being tested by scientific method. However, this is a narrative rather than a systematic review: the style, dose and comparison groups vary greatly between studies, and follow-up is mostly short. Better studies are needed to pin down how large the benefit is.
y6-2: Researchers at Tufts Medicine in the US reviewed the last 12 years of studies on tai chi for chronic musculoskeletal pain in a review published in Current Rheumatology Reports on 9 October 2026: 19 randomised trials with 2,031 participants, plus 34 reviews. The evidence was strongest for knee and hip osteoarthritis: in an analysis combining 28 trials, tai chi improved pain, mobility, function and stiffness compared with groups that did not exercise, and the benefit for pain grew with more frequent and longer weekly practice. Results for fibromyalgia and chronic low back pain are promising but vary widely between studies; for rheumatoid arthritis, the evidence is insufficient.

y6-6: These are averages; not everyone suddenly becomes weaker at 35. Activity cannot stop the decline completely, but it can slow it, and no age is too late to start. People who were active as teenagers kept better fitness into adulthood. The researchers plan to measure the participants again at age 68.
y6-7: In the SPAF study run by Sweden’s Karolinska Institutet, the aerobic fitness, muscular endurance and explosive muscle power of 427 randomly selected people born in 1958 were measured repeatedly over 47 years, from age 16 to 63. Aerobic fitness and muscular endurance peaked between ages 26 and 36 and began to decline in the mid-30s; explosive power peaked even earlier. The decline was slow at first and sped up with age: at 63, performance was on average 30–48% below the peak. The decline was similar in women and men. People who took up regular activity in adulthood increased their physical capacity by about 5–10%.

y6-12: This is an analysis that combines existing reviews; it does not say which exercise suits whom best. The researchers note that this reduction is about 60% larger than the average effect reported for common pain medicines, but that comparison was made across different studies, not head to head. Still, the message is clear: movement is one of the core parts of treating pain.
y6-13: Researchers at Adelaide University in Australia brought together 157 systematic reviews on the effect of exercise on pain: 2,736 randomised trials and 221,279 participants in total. In the analysis, published in PAIN Reports, exercise was linked to reductions in both short-term and long-term pain, including osteoarthritis, migraine, neurological and rheumatic diseases and cancer-related pain. On a 0–10 scale, pain fell by an average of 1.1 points. Aerobic exercise, resistance training, yoga, Pilates and tai chi all showed benefits; lower-intensity programmes and those totalling under 2 hours a week also brought meaningful benefit.
